_readme: THE PROVENANCE REGISTER — [pipeline B-17] Private/requirements/ (was pipeline/04-backend-platform.md, folded into the JSON spec 2026-08-15)
B-17: 'Verification against production is permitted and expected, but every artifact it creates is
provably removed, and the check is mechanical rather than remembered.'
🔴 WHY THE ORIGINAL ACCEPTANCE CRITERION WAS REPLACED. It read: 'a single command reports, per
shared table, the count of rows matching the test-marker convention — and it returns zero.' There
was no test-marker convention, so 'matches the convention' was the EMPTY PREDICATE: the count is 0
on any production state whatsoever, forever. Fill `events` with a million probe rows and it still
returns zero. The criterion was satisfied by the absence of the thing it asked to be built.
THE INVERSION. Instead of counting rows that carry a marker nobody applies, count the rows that
CANNOT BE TRACED TO A RELEASED BUILD. That set has a non-empty complement, probe rows land in it
automatically, and it does not depend on anybody remembering to tag anything.
🔴 AND 'EVERY SHARED TABLE MUST BE EMPTY' IS DEAD ON ARRIVAL. `cron_heartbeat` held 16 legitimate
production rows and `revocation_reasons` 8 seeded reference rows when this register was written.
Emptiness was never the property; ATTRIBUTABILITY is.
Because the columns differ, and pretending otherwise is how a check stops checking. Only `events`
and `consent_artifacts` carry `app_version` (0002_analytics.sql:40, :77). The other seven have no
such column and never will: they are written by the EDGE — a scheduled handler, a merchant-of-record
webhook, a route, or the migration itself — and the edge does not know a client version. So each of
those declares its own marker AND the reason that marker is the honest provenance for that table.
A single portfolio-wide rule would have had to be `app_version`, seven tables would have been exempt,
and the exemptions would have been invisible.
── `alsoResolves` — A SECOND RULE, NEVER A LOOSER FIRST ONE (added 2026-08-28) ─────────────────
A table may carry `alsoResolves: [<resolver id>, …]`. The monitor consults it ONLY for a value the
table's primary `resolver` has already refused, and an acceptance on that footing is PRINTED rather
than counted silently — the same discipline the deployment-witness and manual-deploys acceptances
already follow. Two tables use it: `consent_artifacts` (`e2e-run`, and `store-capture` since
2026-09-23), because the nightly e2e lane and the store capture write there on purpose and B-17's own
premise is that they may; and `pending_erasures` (`erasure-step`, [ADR 087]). ⏱ 2026-09-23: every id
an `alsoResolves` lists must be a key of `resolvers`, which tooling/ci/assert-prod-provenance.mjs checks.
🔴 IT EXISTS SO THAT `released-build` IS NEVER WIDENED. The tempting change was to let it accept
anything containing `+` or `-`; that is the empty predicate again, and it would admit `dev`-class
junk forever. A second resolver has to be declared, named, argued for, and can be read on its own.
⚠️ AND IT IS A REAL COST, NOT A FREE ONE: every value a second resolver admits is a value this
monitor will no longer go red for. An entry belongs here only when something EARLIER and CLOSER to
the writer already fails on the state the monitor would have caught. For `consent_artifacts` that
earlier thing is tooling/e2e/purge.mjs, which since 2026-08-28 hard-fails the nightly the moment it
cannot identify the consent row it was told to delete — and since 2026-09-23 does the same for every
drive of a store capture, whose purge also deletes by the run's own `cap-*` stamp.
GATE    · tooling/ci/assert-prod-provenance.mjs — runs on every push in ci.yml. SECRETLESS, so it
CANNOT SEE PRODUCTION. It asserts only what is checkable from the repo: every table the
migrations create has a rule here, every rule names a column that table really has, every
non-`released-build` rule carries a written reason, and the monitor is wired.
MONITOR · tooling/ops/check-prod-provenance.mjs — runs daily in ops-watch.yml, which holds
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and has no push trigger. It is the ONLY limb that can see a row.
It is a WEAKER RUNG than a gate: green means 'nothing has contradicted this since the
last run', never 'this holds'.
Adding a table to any registered database's migrations without adding a row here FAILS THE GATE. That is
the regression this register exists to catch — B-17's prose named four shared tables and the
migrations create nine, three days apart.
⏱ 2026-09-23 · A SUBMISSION LANE IS A RELEASE LANE, AND ADDING IT DOES NOT WIDEN `released-build`.
The rule above forbids loosening the PREDICATE — the version shape and the witnesses. This adds the
store-submission lanes, which ship real binaries stamped with their own run number, under a witness
STRONGER than the served lane's: a Deployment on that lane's own environment at that full commit whose
`payload` names that very run — `payload.run_id` is the run's id and `payload.workflow` its workflow
file, both written by tooling/ci/record-deployment.mjs from the run's own GITHUB_RUN_ID and
GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF. Binding is by run identity, never by time: a dry run at the same commit, a
re-run of one, or a run whose lifetime overlaps an upload names a different run and is refused.
`dev`, `c6-localprobe`, NULL and a dry run's stamp still fail. Found by ops-watch run 35820464059,
which called the first Play upload's consent row (submit-play.yml run 35787897094, stamped
`1.0.5+0390db6`) unattributable.
`legacyDeploymentBindings` below is the ONE place a payload-less submission Deployment can bind: each
entry maps one Deployment id to one run id, with the workflow, environment and full sha it was measured
at, a date and a reason. It admits no build by itself — the run must still exist, carry that id and
have that head commit. An entry is added only for a Deployment written before its writer carried the
payload, measured with `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/deployments?environment=<env>`.
⏱ 2026-09-26 · EVERY DATABASE, NOT ONE (O-PROVENANCE-WALKS-ONE-DATABASE). The rules sit under `databases.<database_name>`,
each with the `wrangler` config that owns it, its `migrationsDir` and its `tables`. WHICH databases is read from the tree:
tooling/platform-register.json's servingWorker, then each appWorker, and in each Worker's wrangler config every TOP-LEVEL
D1 binding carrying `migrations_dir` (tooling/ci/migration-tables.mjs `registeredD1Databases`). The gate and the monitor
both hold this map to that set, both ways: a database with no entry is COVERAGE LOST, and an entry no config owns is a
finding. `env.<name>` blocks (the store capture's `env.sandbox`) are not production and are never walked. A table whose
columns carry no marker any resolver reads is `exempt`: no `marker`, and a reason that names every one of its columns.

legacyDeploymentBindings.why: The first Play upload (submit-play.yml run_number 5, attempt 1, 21:38:59Z-21:59:43Z on 2026-09-22) recorded this Deployment at 21:59:38Z with `payload: {}`, before record-deployment.mjs wrote the run payload. It is the only Deployment on subscriptiontracker-android-play. Binding it to run id 35787897094 alone means no other run at 0390db6 can resolve through it.

resolvers.operator-minted: The marker value must be a NON-EMPTY provenance string recorded by the operator act that created the row — a commit sha or a register hash. Rows in these tables are neither client-written nor migration-seeded: they are minted by a dated, reviewed human act, so the honest question is not "which build shipped this" but "what state was this minted against". NULL or empty fails, which is the point: a row minted against nothing is a row nobody can review.
resolvers.product-kind: The marker value must be one of the member kinds declared in contracts/entitlement/bundle.js (`MEMBER_KINDS`: every product kind but `bundle`, since a bundle is never a member of one) — the same list tooling/bundle-availability.mjs derives the live-product set from. A value outside it is a row nothing in this tree could have written. Deliberately NOT a join against the product catalogues: a RETIRED product leaves the catalogue while grants that pinned it must keep resolving, so a catalogue join would turn honest history into a false red.
resolvers.released-build: The marker value must be the version string of a build a release lane actually shipped: `<release_line>.<run_number>+<sha7>`, where a run numbered <run_number> whose head commit is <sha7> stands on one of three footings. (1) A SERVED lane in tooling/channel-register.json ran it and the run SUCCEEDED, or it left a GitHub Deployment for <sha7> on a served environment. (2) ⏱ 2026-09-23 — a SUBMISSION lane (a submittable Flutter-app channel's `submission.workflow`) ran it, and a GitHub Deployment at that full commit on that lane's `{app}-<channel>` environment carries a `payload` naming that run (`run_id` = the run's id, `workflow` = the lane's workflow file) — or is a payload-less Deployment that `legacyDeploymentBindings` binds to that run's id; its conclusion is not consulted, because a dry run succeeds and ships nothing, and time is not consulted, because a dry run's lifetime can overlap an upload's Deployment. (3) An attested manual deploy in tooling/ops/manual-deploys.json, accepted only once its commit and its Deployment are both read back. Derived from the GitHub Actions API at read time — never a list in this file (`legacyDeploymentBindings` binds a payload-less Deployment to one run id and admits no build by itself). `dev` (the dart-define default), `c6-localprobe` (the C-6 live probe's literal), NULL and a dry run's stamp all fail, which is the point.
resolvers.live-environment: The marker value must be exactly `live`. Every row in these tables is written by the money rail, which stamps `live` or `sandbox` on purpose ([5]M-12: a sandbox notification is stored so it is auditable and can never write a live entitlement). A verification against production necessarily runs in sandbox, so `sandbox` IS the test marker for this half of the schema — and NULL is worse than either, because it is a row the rail could not attribute at all.
resolvers.cron-job: The marker value must be a job the deployed Worker both DECLARES and USES — the `export const <NAME>_JOB = '<literal>'` set in services/platform/src, the same derivation tooling/ops/check-heartbeats.mjs uses for its completeness limb. A heartbeat row naming a job no deployed code writes is residue from a renamed or deleted job.
resolvers.provider-register: The marker value must be a rail declared in tooling/legal/provider-register.json. A row naming a provider the register does not carry is either a fabricated row or a rail that reached production without a legal record, and both need a human.
resolvers.migration-seed: The marker value must be one of the literals the migrations themselves INSERT into that column. These are reference rows, not data: their provenance is the migration ledger, and any value outside it was put there by hand.
resolvers.e2e-run: The marker value must be exactly `e2e-<run_number>-<sha7>` — lower-case literal prefix `e2e-`, 1-9 digits, `-`, and exactly 7 lower-case hex characters. That is the ONE string .github/workflows/e2e.yml derives into $GITHUB_ENV and passes as `--dart-define=APP_VERSION`, added 2026-08-28 so that the nightly's live-verification rows stop landing as `dev`. It is a NARROW ADDITION to `consent_artifacts` and is registered nowhere else. 🔴 IT IS SHAPE-ONLY AND THEREFORE WEAKER THAN `released-build`, AND IT SAYS SO: it is not checked against the e2e lane's real run history, so a row hand-posted in this shape would resolve. What it cannot admit is the class this register was written against — `dev`, `c6-localprobe`, NULL, a bare `e2e`, an upper-case sha, a full 40-char sha and any released-build string all fail it. ⚠️ AND THE FALSE-NEGATIVE IT WOULD OTHERWISE CREATE IS PAID FOR ELSEWHERE, NOT WAIVED: accepting `e2e-*` means residue from a CRASHED nightly no longer reds ops-watch, which is exactly the incident of 2026-08-27. It is only defensible because tooling/e2e/purge.mjs now HARD-FAILS the moment it cannot identify the consent row it was asked to delete — the nightly goes red at the moment of the failure, on the workflow that owns the residue, instead of a different workflow going red a day later. A row accepted here is also PRINTED on every run rather than passing silently, so the residue stays visible in the monitor's own log.
resolvers.store-capture: ⏱ 2026-09-23. The marker value must be exactly `cap-<run_number>-<sha7>` — lower-case literal prefix `cap-`, 1-9 digits, `-`, and exactly 7 lower-case hex characters — AND a run of .github/workflows/store-screenshots.yml with that run number whose head commit starts with <sha7> must exist, of ANY status (an in-progress capture's rows must not red the ops-watch that reads during it). The stamp is DERIVED by tooling/e2e/app-version-stamp.mjs `captureStamp` from the Actions default env (GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER, GITHUB_SHA, GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF) inside the capture run; the workflow sets nothing. A SECOND resolver for `consent_artifacts` only, and WITNESSED, so it is STRONGER than `e2e-run`'s shape-only check. The capture run set is read on its own and never merged into the runs `released-build` reads, so a capture run cannot lend its number and sha to a release. A local rehearsal's `rehearsal-<epoch>` stamp is DELIBERATELY unwitnessable and stays red. ⚠️ THE FALSE-NEGATIVE IS PAID FOR THE SAME WAY AS `e2e-run`: the capture job's always() purge (tooling/e2e/purge.mjs with E2E_CONSENT_LEDGER) deletes every drive's consent row by anon_id AND every row carrying the stamp, and HARD-FAILS when a drive's id is unresolved; an acceptance here is PRINTED on every run, so a row that survived the purge stays visible. `events` carries NO second resolver: a cap-stamped event means a capture granted analytics, which is a defect and stays red. ⏱ 2026-09-25 — since the capture reaches the sandbox Workers (docs/ci/store-screenshots.md, section "Backend"), a production `cap-*` consent row that this resolver witnesses is a FINDING, not an acceptance: tooling/ops/check-prod-provenance.mjs reports it as "a sandbox lane wrote production" and exits 1. The resolver still runs, so an unwitnessed `cap-*` value keeps its own refusal.
resolvers.erasure-step: ⏱ 2026-09-15 · [ADR 087]. The marker value must be one of the NON-APP erasure steps the platform Worker declares as `export const <NAME>_STEP = '<literal>'` in services/platform/src (today one: `platform:signups`, the launch-list purge in lib/erasure-ledger.ts), read at run time — never a list here. A SECOND resolver for `pending_erasures` only: that table's `app_id` normally names an app (primary `app-catalogue`), and it names a step only when DELETE /v1/account could not confirm the account address and queued the purge for the nightly retry. A step value outside the declared set is residue from a renamed or removed step, and stays unattributable. The `:` cannot occur in an app slug, so a step can never be read as an app.
resolvers.not-reserved-address: The marker column holds an EMAIL ADDRESS, and the monitor NEVER READS IT: the query D1 runs projects each row to `reserved` or `unreserved` inside D1 and returns only a COUNT per bucket, so no address leaves platform_db, reaches a runner or appears in a log. A row resolves when its address is NOT at a domain reserved for testing by RFC 2606 / RFC 6761 — example.com, example.net, example.org and their subdomains, and the .example, .test, .invalid and .localhost names. ⏱ 2026-09-15 · [ADR 087]. ⚠️ DELIBERATELY WEAKER THAN `released-build`, AND IT SAYS SO: it cannot prove a real person signed up, only that the row is not addressed to a place no person receives mail. That is the residue this table actually produces — the 2026-09-15 live rate-limiter probe posted `limiter-probe-2026-09-15@example.com` — and a stronger marker would need a column, which the published promise ("your email address and the time you signed up, and nothing else") forbids.
resolvers.app-catalogue: The marker value must be the slug of an app the factory actually ships, read from tooling/channel-register.json's `apps` list — the same catalogue assert-channel-register.mjs grades its own rows against, never a second list here. For DERIVED tables that carry no build marker of their own. ⚠️ DELIBERATELY WEAKER THAN `released-build`, AND IT SAYS SO: it proves the row belongs to a real app, not that a released build wrote it, so a row derived from a `dev`-stamped event still resolves. That residual is accepted only because the SOURCE table is separately held to `released-build`, and it is recorded here rather than hidden. What it does catch is the state this portfolio has actually produced — rows for an app id nothing ships, i.e. probe residue (`c6-localprobe`).
resolvers.extension-catalogue: ⏱ 2026-09-24 · O-EXTENSION-ACCOUNT-CHECK-UNBUILT. The marker value must be the slug of a browser extension the factory ships, read from extensions/catalog/extensions.json (each entry's `slug`) by its own reader in tooling/ops/check-prod-provenance.mjs (`extensionSlugs`) — never a list here, and never the app catalogue: an extension is not an app, so an app slug must not resolve an extension-keyed row. For the extension account-check tables, which carry no build marker of their own. ⚠️ DELIBERATELY WEAKER THAN `released-build`, AND IT SAYS SO, exactly as `app-catalogue` is: it proves the row belongs to a real extension, not that a released build wrote it. An empty or unreadable catalogue is COULD NOT LOOK, not a finding about the rows.
resolvers.exempt: ⏱ 2026-09-26 · O-PROVENANCE-WALKS-ONE-DATABASE. NOT A RESOLVER, AND IT SAYS SO: the table carries no column any resolver here can read — no build stamp, no app or extension slug, no money world, no closed set a migration seeds — so the monitor does not query it and prints it as exempt on every run. An `exempt` rule declares no `marker`, and its `reason` is 20+ characters and names every column the migrations give the table (tooling/ci/migration-tables.mjs `exemptionProblem`, applied by the gate and by the monitor), so the exemption is an argument about that exact column set and a column added later re-opens it; a table that gains `app_version` must take `released-build` (the gate's limb 5). ⚠️ AN EXEMPT TABLE'S ROWS ARE NOT TRACED AT ALL: residue a live verification leaves there is invisible to this monitor, and removing it is the purge of the harness that wrote it.

events.reason: Carries `app_version` (0002_analytics.sql:40), written straight through from the client envelope by services/platform/src/routes/events.ts. This is the nearest thing to a marker that already existed — C-6's live probe rows carried `app_version: c6-localprobe` — which is why the inversion is cheap here.

consent_artifacts.reason: Carries `app_version` (0002_analytics.sql:77), same writer, same envelope. Append-only by design, so a stray row can never be corrected by an UPDATE — it can only be deleted, which is exactly the disposition B-17 wants proven. ⬜ `alsoResolves` ADDED 2026-08-28 (`e2e-run`); `store-capture` joined it 2026-09-23. From that date .github/workflows/e2e.yml stamps `APP_VERSION=e2e-<run_number>-<sha7>` on the nightly's live verification, so this table legitimately receives rows the release lane did not ship — B-17's own premise is that verification against production is permitted and EXPECTED. Those rows fail `released-build` by construction, and widening `released-build` to admit them is the empty-predicate failure this register's _readme was written against, so the second resolver is a SEPARATE, NARROW one instead. ⏱ 2026-09-23 — the same holds for .github/workflows/store-screenshots.yml, whose live capture drives stamp `cap-<run_number>-<sha7>` (tooling/e2e/app-version-stamp.mjs) and are resolved by the WITNESSED `store-capture`. `resolver` stays `released-build`: it is still the primary rule, assert-prod-provenance.mjs limb 5 requires exactly that of any table carrying `app_version`, and `alsoResolves` is consulted only for a value the primary has already refused.

entitlements.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN AND NEVER WILL HAVE ONE: the row is written by services/platform/src/lib/mor/store.ts from a merchant-of-record notification, not by a client, so no app build is involved and there is no version to record. `provider_environment` (0004_money_rail.sql:73) is the column that answers the same question — which money world produced this row. It is the highest-consequence table in the set: B-17's own first-revenue note is that a test entitlement row in production is a free Pro unlock nobody notices, and a NULL here is precisely such a row.

cron_heartbeat.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the Worker's own scheduled handler (services/platform/src/scheduled.ts), which has no client and no app build. `job` is its only self-describing column, and it is a closed set the source declares. THIS TABLE IS WHY 'shared tables must be empty' had to be abandoned — its 16 rows are the instrument working, not residue.

provider_notifications.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the MoR webhook (0004 section B) before anything interprets it. `environment` (0004_money_rail.sql:161) is stamped by the rail itself. This is the one non-pseudonymous store in platform_db — it keeps the buyer's name, email and billing country VERBATIM — so a sandbox row lingering here is a real person's data retained for no reason, not just untidiness.

provider_accounts.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN and no `environment` column either: the row is DERIVED from a notification rather than received, so the environment lives on the notification it was derived from. `provider` is the column it does carry, and it is a closed set the legal register owns. The row links a person to a subscription, which is why it deliberately carries `user_id` and joins the erasure sweep.

provider_payment_links.reason: ⏱ 2026-10-02 · PR #1149 ruling item 2. NO `app_version` COLUMN: the row is DERIVED from a signed `subscription.charged` notification (a Razorpay payment id → the subscription it charged) by services/platform/src/lib/mor/store.ts linkPayment. `environment` (0025_provider_payment_links.sql) is stamped from the destination's money world, the same column unclaimed_payments carries; a sandbox row here would resolve a sandbox refund against a live subscription, so a non-live row in production is a finding.

unclaimed_payments.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the webhook when money arrived and no account could be resolved. `environment` (0004_money_rail.sql) is stamped by the rail. A sandbox row here is the most misleading kind of residue in the whole schema — it is evidence of an unresolved real payment, and a fake one wastes exactly the investigation the table exists to make possible.

signups.reason: ⏱ 2026-09-15 · [ADR 087]. NO `app_version` COLUMN, AND THERE CANNOT BE ONE: the rows are written by the nikatru.com Pages Function (sites/nikatru/functions/api/subscribe.js) from a website form, which has no app build, and sites/nikatru/privacy.html promises the table holds the email address and the signup time and nothing else — so no marker column of any kind may be added. `email` is therefore the marker, read only through the `not-reserved-address` projection, which counts rows addressed to test domains without ever returning an address.

pending_erasures.reason: ⏱ 2026-09-15 · [ADR 081]. NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by DELETE /v1/account (services/platform/src/routes/account.ts) from the authenticated session when an app could not be reached, and deleted by the nightly erasure retry when the erasure completes. `app_id` is NOT NULL and is always an app APP_ERASURE_ENDPOINTS names, i.e. a catalogue app, so a row naming anything else was not written by this route.

cancellation_requests.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the cancellation route (0005) from the authenticated session, not from an app envelope. `environment` is NOT NULL in the DDL for the same [5]M-12 reason as the rest of the rail, so the marker is guaranteed present and only its VALUE can be wrong.

bundle_grants.reason: THE SAME ANSWER `entitlements` GIVES, AND FOR THE SAME REASON — one vocabulary, one set of readers. No `app_version` column and never will have one: the row is written by the money rail from a merchant-of-record notification or a server-side receipt pull, not by a client, so no app build is involved and there is no version to record. `provider_environment` (0009_bundle_grants.sql section A) is the column that answers the same question — which money world produced this row. 🔴 IT CARRIES THE SAME FIRST-REVENUE CONSEQUENCE AS `entitlements`, MULTIPLIED: a test bundle grant in production is a free Pro unlock across EVERY member product, not one, and a NULL here is precisely such a row. ⚠️ THE TWO EXEMPT SOURCES DO NOT BREAK THE RULE: `promo_code` and `owner_comp` grants carry no receipt, but they are still written by this Worker in this environment and still stamp `provider_environment` — the exemption is from a RECEIPT, never from the money world.
bundle_grants._note: As of 2026-09-09 this table has zero rows in production; the rule exists before the first one, which is the only time it is free.

bundle_sources.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN AND NO WRITER AT ALL: reference data seeded by 0009_bundle_grants.sql section B and extendable only by an additive INSERT in a later migration. Nothing in the running system writes it, so 'traced to a released build' is the wrong question — the right one is 'is this row in the migration ledger'. Same shape as `revocation_reasons`, and the same reason emptiness could never have been the rule: it has seven rows the day it is created.

feature_sets.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN, BECAUSE NEITHER A CLIENT NOR THE MONEY RAIL WRITES THIS, AND IT IS NOT SEEDED EITHER — which is why it needs its own resolver rather than borrowing one that would fit badly. A feature-set version is MINTED by a dated, reviewed operator act ([ADR 057] §4: adding a product to the bundle is forward-only and explicit), and `minted_from` is the commit or register hash that act recorded. A row with a NULL or empty `minted_from` is a version somebody created by hand against no reviewed state — and because a `sellable` version's members are frozen and grants PIN it, such a row silently defines what a stranger bought. Reusing `migration-seed` here would have been the empty-predicate failure this register's _readme was written against: no migration seeds this table, so the predicate would range over nothing and print clean forever.

feature_set_members.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN — no client build touches these rows. THE MEMBER ROWS ARE THE RESOLUTION OF A PURCHASE, so an unattributable one is the sharpest failure in this migration: a member row silently added or removed changes what an EXISTING grant unlocks, with no revocation, no notification and no trace. There is no version string and no environment on these rows; what there is, is the category the slug came from, and `product_kind` outside the declared member kinds (`MEMBER_KINDS` in contracts/entitlement/bundle.js) means a row nothing in the tree could have written. ⚠️ THE STRONGER CHECK — that `product_slug` names a product in `catalog/apps.json` or `extensions/catalog/extensions.json` — is deliberately NOT this rule: a RETIRED product legitimately leaves the catalogue while old grants must keep resolving it, so a catalogue join would turn honest history into a false red. That check belongs to the mint, not to the monitor.

revocation_reasons.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN and no writer at all: this is REFERENCE DATA seeded by 0004_money_rail.sql:282 and extended only by an additive INSERT in a later migration. Nothing in the running system writes it, so 'traced to a released build' is the wrong question — the right one is 'is this row in the migration ledger'. Its 8 rows are the second reason emptiness could never have been the rule.

events_daily.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN — the rollup DROPS it, deliberately: 0007_events_rollup.sql keeps only the five grain columns the [11]E-11 numbers need, and the build string is not one of them. So the strongest marker is genuinely absent rather than waived, and `app_id` is the only self-describing column that survives aggregation. 🔴 THE TEMPTING RULE HERE WAS 'provenance is INHERITED from `events`', and it was rejected because NO ROW COULD EVER VIOLATE IT — an assertion that cannot fail inflates the covered-table count while checking nothing, which is worse than declaring none. `app-catalogue` can fail: a row whose `app_id` names no shipped app is probe residue.

rollup_state.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN and no app at all: this is a CONTROL, not data — one row naming the last day the rollup fully consumed, which the events sweep reads to decide how far it may delete. 0007_events_rollup.sql seeds the only legitimate value (`events_daily`) with an INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so the migration ledger IS its provenance and 'traced to a released build' is the wrong question, exactly as it is for revocation_reasons one entry up. A `rollup` value outside the seeded set was put there by hand.
